title: SiriuS: Self-improving Multi-agent Systems via Bootstrapped Reasoning

selection.evidence: MASS (lee2026-mass-self-supervision) names it as the prior method that trains on selected multi-agent traces: the closest precedent.

cost.compute_notes: 21-page PDF: Secs 1-4 and App. C read, competitive-setting results skimmed. Repo cloned (230 KB). s01 under 1 s.

triggers: experience library of successful multi-agent trajectories
one shared model vs per-role models

claims.statement: SiriuS (fine-tune each agent on its own successful or augmented trajectories) consistently outperforms single-agent, STaR, a prompted multi-agent system (CoMM) and TextGrad on College Physics, College Chemistry and PubMedQA, by 2.86-21.88%.
claims.scope: gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 and gpt-4o-mini-2024-07-18 via the OpenAI fine-tuning API, temperature 0, one run. Test sets: physics 107, chemistry 65, PubMedQA 500 (Table 6).

our_assessment.why: All 30 printed percentages decode to integer counts at the stated test sizes, so the tables are self-consistent. 'Consistently outperforms' rests on margins of 1-7 questions on the 107- and 65-question sets, single runs, and no intervals: the Wilson CIs of SiriuS and the best baseline overlap in all six cells. The large, believable effect is against single-agent STaR on PubMedQA (+52/500 for gpt-3.5). That comparison does not match compute: three model calls against one. Against the untrained prompted multi-agent system (CoMM), training adds 12-14/500. That is the cleanest estimate of what SFT on the system's own successful multi-agent traces buys over the same multi-agent prompt.

claims.statement: Role-specific fine-tuned models beat one shared model fine-tuned on all roles' data ('FT on One Base LLM'): PubMedQA 74.2 vs 70.4 (gpt-3.5), 73.4 vs 72.0 (4o-mini); actor-critic overall accuracy 50.6 vs 43.6 and 66.8 vs 59.6.

our_assessment.why: The gpt-3.5 difference (19/500) and both actor-critic differences (35-36/500) are well above noise for one run. The 4o-mini PubMedQA difference (7/500) is not. This bears on MASS, which deliberately trains ONE shared model on orchestrator and worker windows together. SiriuS's evidence points the other way for small fixed-role systems. The settings differ (3 fixed roles on QA vs open delegation on coding), so it is a tension to note, not a refutation.

claims.statement: A second SiriuS iteration (regenerate the experience library with the fine-tuned system, fine-tune again) gives marginal further gains.

our_assessment.why: The paper calls it marginal, which is right; at 1-4 of 500 it is indistinguishable from zero. It is the recursive step, and it is flat, which is consistent with MASS's own L0 -> L1 held-out result (c1 there).

checked.result: All 30 Table 3 cells and 12 Table 4 cells decode to integer counts at n = 107 / 65 / 500; no failures.

68 Python files for the three settings. Data shipped: dataset/phy_train.jsonl with 5 lines. No test sets, no experience libraries, no outputs, and no fine-tuned model ids. Reproduction needs the OpenAI fine-tuning API on gpt-3.5-turbo-0125; whether that is still offered was not checked.

open_questions: Paired per-question outcomes (SiriuS vs CoMM) would turn the 12-14/500 PubMedQA margin into a McNemar test; are they recoverable?
Does the per-role vs shared-model advantage survive at larger model sizes or open-ended delegation (MASS's regime)?
